Currently I watch movies through DLNA from a windows 7 machine with windows media player and do not a have a good system for backing up or storing important documents or family photos. I think that I would like to set up a computer to dedicated to handle these things, but I don't know where to begin. I have an XP era machine that ran well when I unplugged it a few years back and an unused Raspberry pi model B. Aside from perhaps a new hard drive or second hand router, I don't really have much of a budget for this project. I would like to be able to access the movies, etc from multiple DLNA capable TV's in the house and would like to be able to handle the pictures/ documents from any computer in the house. I have a Actiontec MI424WR router. I also have limited experience with Linux.

For the actual questions:

  1. Is the hardware I have adequate for what I would like to do?

  2. Should I look into getting a second router?

  3. Is Kodi/ XBMC appropriate for what I want?

  4. If i use the old desktop, which Linux distros should I consider?

  5. What are some good resources for figuring this stuff out on my own?

Sorry for the heap of questions, and thanks in advance.
Could use some help setting up a file/ media server

Is Kodi/ XBMC appropriate for what I want?

Kodi/XBMC is a media-player, you could use it on your Raspberry Pi to create something like a little set-top box. Your TVs already support DLNA so you don't need that. What you want is a media-server that supports DLNA like MediaTomb or ReadyMedia/miniDLNA.

Is the hardware I have adequate for what I would like to do?

It's not optimal but enough.

If i use the old desktop, which Linux distros should I consider?

Any modern distro that's suitable for servers should do the trick, Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora...

Then you can install

  • MediaTomb or ReadyMedia/miniDLNA to get the videos to your TVs

  • Samba for network storage

  • and maybe ownCloud

You could also run this on your raspberry, in that case I'd use Raspbian or Debian.

Should I look into getting a second router?

Some routers can use an external harddisk and support DLNA and Samba (e.g. anything that runs a DD-WRT and has a USB-port). But I don't know how good the performance is.

What are some good resources for figuring this stuff out on my own?

It's easy to find answers to specific question, e.g. "How do install miniDLNA on a raspberry pi?". Finding out what is possible is a bit harder. You could look at the Synology Diskstations and then find out how you can get the same features on your existing hardware.

If you think this kind of thing isn't serious, then you know nothing about North Korea. They have been living under the threat of nuclear attack by the US since during the war, and yes, we most certainly did threaten them with that a number of times (not that it would have made much of a difference during the war since we bombed the country to dust with our conventional bombs anyway). Their number one goal since the war has been to find a counter to this ability, and for a while they had to focus on overwhelming conventional forces and the "mad man theory". They eventually developed chemical weapons and biological weapons, which they have literally tons of, and that has helped them feel more secure, but never completely safe. That's why they went hard at developing nuclear weapons as soon as they were able, and that's why it's a pretty big deal that they now have nukes they can actually use, as in warheads (yes, they have warheads; all experts on this subject agree that they're at that point already). So what does this mean exactly?

First of all, it doesn't mean that North Korea can beat the US in a nuclear exchange. The North is still developing ICBM's and SLBM's, but there are no barriers to them producing effective models of those weapons, so we can safely assume that they will be operational within the next 1-5 years, depending on setbacks. They can, however, use their SRBM's, MRBM's, and LRBM's to hit targets all over East Asia and the Pacific, including all of Korea, Japan, and even Guam. This puts a lot of serious US hardware and personnel in the cross-hairs, and that threat is real. No, we cannot shoot down every single missile they try to shoot. Our anti-missile systems don't work that way (when they even work). North Korean ballistic missiles are not very accurate, but with nukes that doesn't matter nearly as much. It's safe to say that they could nuke any target in South Korea with ease.

But will they? Probably not. Nukes are not exactly a "usable weapon" for them, mostly because of the US nuclear threat. Their nukes are almost entirely there to deter, not to be used. With them, they could deter the US from using its nukes, which we'd rather not do anyway, but now we have even more reason not to. They could also deter any large scale amphibious landings, which are already nigh on impossible with modern military capabilities (and the fact that much of Korea's coastline is rocky or muddy and thus unsuitable for landings). But most importantly, they can use their nukes to bring the South and US to the table on their terms and end any future war before they start losing, which is something they could never have been able to do previously. So their nukes give them some pretty serious strategic results without even using them (like most countries' nukes). This could simply make them think they're untouchable so they don't have to worry about being invaded, which means they can divert resources from their conventional forces to other aspects of their economy, or it could make them think a war is now winnable, giving them the final impetus to give it a shot, lest their country collapse due to its own systemic failures and the outside world eroding their control of information (and thus brainwashing).

So if you think this is all business as usual, you don't have the slightest clue about what's really happening.
